title: Circles of curvature and osculating frames: how much does the path bend here?
summary: At chosen points of a curve the best-fitting circle (the osculating circle) is drawn, with its centre and radius, together with the tangent and normal directions. A small circle means a sharp bend; a huge circle means nearly straight.

media.alt: A teal sine-like curve with three circles tangent to it: one solid amber circle at the crest labelled R = 1.25 and two dashed blue circles labelled R = 2.65 and R = 1.58, each with a radius line to its centre mark, an amber tangent arrow and a rose normal arrow.
media.caption: Reference render of class F3.6 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How much does the path bend here?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y in the plane, equal scale (-0.5 to 7 and -3.4 to 3.4). The curve is y = 0.8 sin x. Circles are drawn at x = pi/2 (amber), 2.35 and 4.3 (blue dashed). Amber arrow: unit tangent T. Rose arrow: normal N. White line: radius from the point to the centre (the plus sign).
look_at: Which circle is smallest and where is the curve bending most sharply?
On which side of the curve does each centre lie? It is the inside of the bend.
At the middle point (x = 2.35) the circle is large. What does that say about the curve there?
How are T and N related?
as_drawn: Radii: R = 1.25 at the crest x = pi/2 (curvature 0.8), 2.65 at x = 2.35 (curvature 0.377), 1.58 at x = 4.3 (curvature 0.633).
Axes are equal, so the circles look like circles and R can be read from the picture. The legend says amber is the current point.
The big dashed circle at x = 2.35 leaves the frame at the bottom: R = 2.65 is cut off, a limitation of any curvature-circle plot near an inflection.
read_the_figure.proves: The size of the local bend at the plotted points and which way the curve turns. It says nothing about points between those marked, and the osculating circle matches the curve only to second order.
if_wrong: Unequal axes: circles become ellipses and R is unreadable.
Radius arrows missing: the circle floats with no stated link to the point.
Circles at one point only: the variation of curvature along the curve is hidden.

terms.meaning: How fast the direction of the curve turns per unit of length.
The reciprocal of the curvature: the radius of the circle that best fits the curve.
The circle that touches the curve at a point with the same tangent and curvature (a second-order fit).
Unit vectors along the curve and perpendicular to it, pointing to the inside of the bend.
The pair (T, N) moving along the curve; in 3D it also includes a binormal.
A point where the bend changes sign, so the curvature is zero and R is infinite.

remember: The centre lies on the normal, at distance R, on the concave side.
At an inflection kappa = 0 and R is infinite.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each circle is a line mark whose size is the radius of curvature. Its centre is a plus sign; a white arrow connects the point of tangency to it. The two arrows at the point are the frame: amber tangent, rose normal. Highlighting the current point in amber and drawing the others dashed distinguishes focus from context.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Curvature is an abstract number, but a circle is a shape the eye knows well. The circle that hugs the curve most closely makes the bend visible: a tight circle is a sharp bend, a large circle a gentle one. Placing the circle on the concave side shows the direction of the turn. The tangent and normal show the frame that the circle is attached to.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: If the aspect ratio is not 1 the circle becomes an ellipse and R cannot be read. A circle fits to second order only, so it can cross the curve (at an inflection it does). The very large circles near inflections run off the plot. A few circles can hide where the curvature changes fast. Computing curvature from noisy samples amplifies the noise.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Radius arrows tie the circle to a point and give the reader a length to measure. Frames at several points show how the direction field turns. Equal aspect makes both statements honest. This render has all three, with the highlighted point in amber.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: To see the curvature everywhere plot kappa against arc length, or colour the curve by kappa. The evolute (the locus of centres) summarises all the circles at once. For 3D curves use the Frenet frame with torsion, or a parallel-transport frame for twist-free curves.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Colour the curve by curvature with a colour bar and draw the evolute as a dotted line; add the point of zero curvature at x = pi and show its tangent line crossing the curve.

steps.title: Curvature of a graph
steps.note: For y = 0.8 sin x: y' = 0.8 cos x, y'' = -0.8 sin x. At x = pi/2: y' = 0 and kappa = 0.8, R = 1.25. At x = 2.35: kappa = 0.377, R = 2.65. At x = 4.3: kappa = 0.633, R = 1.58. All match the render's labels.

steps.title: Where the curvature vanishes
steps.note: At the inflection x = pi the curve crosses its own tangent line and no finite circle fits, which is why the plot has no circle there.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) where is the bend sharpest? (2) Where is the centre of the amber circle relative to the crest? (3) How big is the circle at x = 2.35?

solution.text: At the crest and the trough: the radii 1.25 and 1.58 are the smallest of the three circles. The crest, with y'' = -0.8, is the sharpest of these.
Below the crest, at (pi/2, 0.8 - 1.25) = (1.57, -0.45): the centre is on the concave side, one radius away along the normal.
R = 2.65, more than twice the crest radius: the curve is flatter there, close to the inflection at x = pi.

worked.answer: Sharpest at the crest (R = 1.25); the centre sits 1.25 below it on the normal; R = 2.65 near the inflection.

checks.q: What is the radius of curvature of a circle of radius 3 at any point?
checks.answer: 3: a circle's best-fit circle is itself, curvature 1/3.

checks.q: At a crest y' = 0 and y'' = -0.5. What is R?
Where on a sine curve is the radius of curvature infinite and what does the osculating circle look like there?
checks.answer: At the inflections (x = n pi). No circle: it degenerates to the tangent line.
